title: "Something's really possible" - Mass Effect cast rally around fan efforts to save the franchise on the first N7 Day after BioWare's shock closure
author: Kaan Serin
content:
I'm Commander Shepard and this is my favorite video on the internet.

This N7 Day was the first without developer BioWare around, but fans of the Mass Effect series didn't let 7th November go by quietly. The community managed to get several notable Mass Effect actors to lend their voice to the increasingly loud 'SaveMassEffect' movement.

In the weeks since BioWare's shock closure and Mass Effect Universe's cancellation, the community-organised We Are Mass Effect group have put up billboards in Times Square, a mobile billboard outside BioWare Edmonton's former office and much more while directing attention to an online petition.

Today is a very special day for Mass Effect fans. We've worked incredibly hard to bring together most of the original Mass Effect trilogy's voice cast to share a very important message with you. We need to #SaveMassEffect. https://t.co/FOp0qp4wBI

— We are Mass Effect - #SaveMassEffect (@WeAreMassEffect) November 7, 2026

And for the series' annual celebration, the group managed to get a sizable portion of the Mass Effect cast to join in. Commander Shepard actors Jennifer Hale and Mark Meer, original trilogy composer Sam Hulick, Garrus' Brandon Keener, Jack's Courtnay Taylor, Tali'Zorah's Ash Sroka, Thane's Keythe Farley and many more all showed up in a two-minute video to help potentially salvage the series - sometimes in character.

"When we heard about the formal closing of Boware, I felt weirdly hopeful," Hale said in a separate interview with IGN. "I can't explain it. I just got so weirdly hopeful. My first thought, of course, was for the devs and all the people. And then I just closed my eyes and crossed my fingers and I said, 'I feel something's possible. You know, something's really possible.'"

The other half of Commander Shepard, Mark Meer, noted that "this didn't all just happen in the last 10 days." Near yearly layoffs at EA had slowly trimmed multiple BioWare teams down, sometimes even affecting studio veterans who had been at the company for decades.

"A lot of senior writers within the last year or two were let go. People who had been there from the very beginning. Again, people who had built that company from the ground up, who built the bones of it, who made those games that had captured people so much right back from the 1990s," Meer said.

title: Lean Muscle Mass Isn’t a Cure-All for Metabolic Health - Nautilus
content:
You’ve probably heard it your entire adult life—building lean muscle mass is one of the best things you can do for your health. After all, in addition to boosting physical strength and burning calories, lean muscle mass also pulls glucose from the blood and helps protect against diabetes. But now a new study published in The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism is challenging that conventional wisdom.

A team of nutritional and chronic disease researchers from Louisiana State University analyzed health data from close to 60,000 adults (between the ages of 37 and 73) enrolled in the U.K. Biobank study. They focused on those who had undergone MRI and low-level X-ray scans capable of determining their fat-free mass, a commonly used proxy for lean muscle mass. 

Read more: “People With This Neanderthal Hormone Receptor Have More Muscle Mass”

The team then investigated the association between fat-free mass and adverse health outcomes, like developing a metabolic disorder and elevated glycated hemoglobin (for connoisseurs of diabetes pharmaceutical ads, this is the HbA1C they’re always singing about). They also assessed different measures of fat-free mass, like visceral adiposity (abdominal and organ fat) and fat infiltration within muscle tissue. 

The results painted a messy picture. For example, higher total fat-free mass (and fat-free mass adjusted for height) was actually associated with a slightly higher likelihood of developing metabolic syndromes and elevated HbA1C. On the other hand, a higher proportion of body weight made up of fat-free mass was associated with a lower likelihood of developing these adverse outcomes. 

“The findings suggest that muscle quantity alone may not provide a complete picture of metabolic health and that where fat is stored in the body is an important part of the story,” study author Sri Lakshmi S. Devarakonda said in a statement.

Drilling down into the data, the team found that visceral fat seemed to have the strongest influence. Those with the same total fat-free mass but more fat around their abdomens and organs were more likely to experience the adverse outcomes. Fatty infiltration into muscle showed the same pattern, albeit slightly weaker.  

“Our findings suggest that we need to look beyond the amount of fat-free mass a person has to better understand their metabolic health,” study author Candida Rebello explained. “Where fat is stored in the body matters, particularly fat around internal organs and fat that accumulates within muscle tissue. These different patterns of fat distribution can influence the relationship between fat-free mass and metabolic risk, underscoring the importance of considering the quality and composition of body tissues, not just their quantity, when studying metabolic health.”

Does any of this mean you should avoid building lean muscle mass? Definitely not. It’s still one of the best things you can do for your health. It’s just not a panacea.

title: The Art of Letting Go
author: Krista Stevens
content:
For The American Scholar, Lisa Russ Spaar offers us beautiful litany of loss in all its various shapes and forms. From those we love to objects like keys, from our teeth to our moral compass, Spaar takes a close look at what we go through when we experience loss at various times in our lives, and how losses tend to stack up as we age.

I’ve informally polled several friends, colleagues, and family members about their first remembered losses. For most, it was when a milk tooth fell out, usually around the age of six. (Surely there are primal reasons many of us dream throughout our lifetimes about our teeth, as important as they are to speaking, eating.) More than 20 years ago, one of my talented undergraduates, Molly, wrote a poem about losing her first tooth while sledding in winter. Upon tonguing the little bloody socket that remained, she wrote, “I taste my death.” That line has haunted me over the decades. Again, our bodies: made for loss. Language: our ability to articulate what that might mean.

I often wonder what was happening in my late mother’s mind as she sank, over a period of 10-plus years, into the tangled ambages of dementia. She lost the names of things and people. She lost any memory of who we were, those of us who cared for her, even her devoted husband, my father. She finally even forgot that she was not only an alcoholic with a fifth of Scotch hidden in the breadbox but also a chain smoker, though she’d occasionally hold a drinking straw to her lips and take a long, deep drag.

title: Famous Fossil Could be Rosetta Stone for Hidden Hominin Diversity - Nautilus
content:
The discovery of the Taung child’s skull in 1924 was a seismic moment in understanding human origins. It was the first Australopithecus specimen ever found. As such, it’s the holotype of the group—the standard measuring stick future specimens were judged by. Now those specimens are coming under renewed scrutiny in a study published in npj Palaeoecosystems. 

An international team of paleobiologists decided to give the Taung child’s noggin a fresh look, and the more they looked, the more discrepancies they found. By comparing the rate of tooth mineralization with chimpanzees, gorillas, humans, and other fossils, the team determined the skull likely belonged to a child (not a juvenile as the original investigating anthropologist surmised). Analysis of the dentine-enamel junction (where the tooth’s hard shell meets its chewy center), revealed a resemblance to Paranthropus robustus, a more ape-like hominin that likely originated after Australopithecus.

Read more: “What Made Early Humans Smart”

Focusing on the braincase, the researchers found other discrepancies. Using chimp and gorilla skull growth as a guide, they compared digitally reconstructed skulls found in the same region and purported to belong to Australopithecus to the Taung child’s braincase. They found that the size and shape of the Taung child’s skull indicate it could have grown into a hominin resembling some of the Australopithecus specimens, but not others.

In other words, the team’s modeling indicates there was a lot more variation among hominins living in the area at the time, and lumping them all into Australopithecus may downplay this diversity. Their investigation of the paleoclimate at the time paints a picture of a region in flux, and they hypothesize these shifts were fueling hominin diversity. As wet and dry cycles continually remodeled the region, hominin populations expanded and contracted, confronting new pathogens and predators, diverging, and interbreeding, according to their theory.

“For over 100 years, we assumed the Taung Child was just one of many similar fossils from the era,” study author Gabriele Macho of Vrije Universiteit Brussel said in a statement. “Our findings turn that on its head. The human family tree wasn’t a neat, straight trunk—it was a chaotic, tangled bush driven by climate shifts.”

Of course, it’s important to note it’s merely a hypothesis. Still, if the past 20 years have taught us anything, it’s that our family tree has more branches than we previously thought.

title: The Downfall of a Top Cop
author: Longreads
content:
Alessio Perrone and Berber Verpoest | The Atavist Magazine | October 2026 | 2,080 words (7 minutes)

This is an excerpt from issue no. 181, “The Rise and Fall of a Super-Cop.”

The shipping container came from Costa Rica, and it was supposed to hold timber. When it arrived in the Belgian city of Antwerp in October 2019, the steel box with tracking number TCKU1048144 was loaded into what looked like a massive game of Tetris: As Europe’s second-largest port, handling some 290 million metric tons of cargo every year, Antwerp holds tens of thousands of shipping containers at any moment, painted in bright hues and arranged in long, neat rows. From the outside, nothing seemed amiss with TCKU1048144, which is exactly what the drug traffickers who’d packed it intended.

Cocaine had been flooding into Antwerp for at least a decade. After Mexican cartels took over the U.S. market, Colombian traffickers looked to Europe, and Antwerp’s port provided them with readymade infrastructure to shuttle their product onto the continent. The cocaine trade warped life in the city. As gangs fought for control, Antwerp was rocked by car bombings, shootings, and other violence. Local media reported on houses battered by grenades as the worst of the city’s underworld attempted to intimidate rivals and snitches. Corruption spread, with trafficking networks paying off port workers, cops, hospital staff—anyone they needed to look the other way.

The Atavist, our sister publication, publishes one deeply reported, elegantly designed story each month. Support The Atavist by becoming a member.

Customs agents found themselves on the front lines of an escalating war, trying to keep cocaine out of Belgium against what seemed like impossible odds. Antwerp’s government had boosted funding for personnel, technology, and other investigative resources, helping customs increase the amount of cocaine it seized each year; the figure more than doubled between 2016 and 2019. Still, European demand for coke was stratospheric, and suppliers were determined to meet it. Powder just kept coming.

On October 28, container TCKU1048144 was selected for X-ray inspection. Containers moving through Antwerp’s port can be designated for a scan at random or for any number of logistical reasons, including improper documentation or suspicious shipping information. The X-ray showed that there was timber inside TCKU1048144, as its paperwork indicated, but agents spotted something else beneath the wood—bags, from the look of it. They opened the container’s heavy doors and found taped-up slabs of cocaine, 2,792 kilograms’ worth. There was also a counterfeit container seal, left by the South American traffickers for the shipment’s European recipients. By resealing the box after removing the drugs, the criminals could make it look as though no one had tampered with TCKU1048144.

Law enforcement decided to let the container continue on to the destination indicated on its paperwork: Maasmechelen, a sleepy town sixty miles southeast of Antwerp. They hoped that this tactic would help them identify and eventually arrest key players in the trafficking network. Customs removed the cocaine, resealed the container, then kept watch over it. The next evening, a driver arrived to pick it up. Law enforcement followed him, but instead of heading toward Maasmechelen, he went north, speeding to the Dutch border. He crossed over and stopped at a warehouse in Zevenbergen, a small city on the Rhine estuary. Outside were several vehicles, including an Audi SUV.

As police watched from a distance, they got a look at the man in the Audi. He was elderly, with steely blue eyes and dark hair. It didn’t take long to identify him. In fact, plenty of people in Belgian law enforcement knew him by sight. His name was Willy Van Mechelen, and once upon a time, he’d been the most famous cop in the country.

Chapter 1

Willy Karel Ferdinand Van Mechelen was born in 1943 into a Catholic family in a middle-class suburb of Antwerp. He spent much of his childhood at his grandfather’s mill in a hamlet in the Kempen, an area between Antwerp and the Dutch border known for its farms and wetlands. Van Mechelen was an exuberant, rebellious boy. When his peers dared him to climb onto a windmill’s rotating blades, he would race to do it. If a priest told him to be quiet during mass, he would storm out of church. According to a memoir he published in 1997, he and his two brothers never caused any serious trouble, but they got up to so much mischief that they became known to their neighbors as “the Dalton brothers,” after a fabled gang of outlaws in the American frontier. (In addition to that memoir, this article is based on dozens of hours of interviews with sources, hundreds of pages of court documents, and several books written by Van Mechelen’s contemporaries.)

During his senior year of high school, Van Mechelen decided to drop out. His father, who worked as a gendarme, had acquaintances at a shipping agency in Antwerp and secured his son a position clearing goods through customs. The job wasn’t exactly adrenaline pumping, even if obtaining stamps from Belgian customs sometimes required greasing the right palms. But Van Mechelen was able to spend his days outdoors, roaming among the terminals of the city’s huge port.

When he turned 18, he began his mandatory military service, and the army gave him direction and purpose. He became a paratrooper and deployed to Burundi, which at that point was still part of a Belgian colony. After fifteen months, he returned to the shipping company a changed man. He was more confident but also more impatient, easily frustrated by older colleagues he would later dismiss as “mummies” who only talked about retirement.

One day a customs agent asked him for a larger than usual bribe. Van Mechelen was unfazed and handed over the banknotes. Back in the office, his boss didn’t thank or reimburse him. Instead he lectured Van Mechelen on how to do his job properly—and did so in French instead of Dutch, the language everyone spoke in Antwerp. Van Mechelen thought that his boss was talking down to him, and he was furious. He grabbed a lectern and hurled it across the room. When he went home, he expressed an interest in his father’s line of work for the first time. Might the national police have a position for him? “That’s how I became a gendarme,” Van Mechelen wrote in his memoir, “out of rage.”

He joined the force in the late 1960s and was assigned to the mounted division, a position he detested for not seeing enough action. Eventually, he became a shooting instructor for the anti-terror squad and then joined a special unit in charge of Antwerp’s most challenging criminal investigations. The unit was known as the BOB, short for Bewakings- en Opsporingsbrigade, or Surveillance and Investigation Brigade.

Belgian law enforcement at the time operated with so few checks and balances that it more or less did as it pleased. In robbery cases where insurance companies offered rewards to informants if their tips contributed to the recovery of loot, cops sometimes roped in civilians after locating stolen items, allowing so-called informants to claim the money and then split it with the officers. The scheme was lucrative but illegal. “There was a bit of a cowboy mentality,” said Jean-Charles Verwaest, a retired journalist.

Complicating matters was the fact that Belgium had three distinct police services: the gendarmerie, a national force under the authority of the country’s interior and defense ministries; the judicial police, which reported to public prosecutors’ offices; and the municipal police, the equivalent of local law enforcement in the U.S. The gendarmerie and the judicial police in particular were locked in a power struggle. They often refused to share intelligence or even acknowledge each other’s authority. Investigations were duplicated or sabotaged, and suspects slipped through cracks widened by ego and pride. The turf struggle reached a peak in the 1980s, becoming known as the guerre des flics, or “cop war.”

Van Mechelen learned the rules of battle early. On his first case with the BOB, he let a more senior colleague drive to the crime scene, only to discover that the judicial police had arrived first and staked their claim to the investigation. “That was my first lesson at the BOB,” he later wrote. “Always get behind the wheel yourself.”

Van Mechelen quickly made a name for himself. He was the kind of man who could have a pint with anyone, and often picked up the tab when he did. Tall and broad shouldered, he cut such an imposing figure that people sometimes compared him to the Belgian comic-book character Jerom, who has superhuman strength. He became known for shows of force and for refusing to take guff from anyone. Once, during a raid, he flung a man through a ground-floor window for the offense of mocking him. “Everyone knew where the line was then,” he later wrote.

Van Mechelen could also be clever. “He was the best detective in the BOB, there’s no getting away from that,” said Walter De Smedt, a former investigative judge who led inquiries into organized crime in Antwerp and often chose to work with Van Mechelen. In those days police officers didn’t specialize. They had to do it all: investigative work, raids, interrogations. “Only Van Mechelen was very good at all of them,” De Smedt said. “If you assigned a case to him, you always got something back.”

Van Mechelen developed his own way of handling the various crimes that afflicted Antwerp, from prostitution rackets to contraband smuggling to violent robberies. When he raided a bar or restaurant during a BOB operation, he scribbled down the name of every person there, noting who was sitting with whom. Over time he developed extensive knowledge of Antwerp’s underworld. “If a robbery happened and we caught one of the perpetrators, all we had to do was check in the file catalog with whom he had been sitting in the bar the days before,” he wrote in his memoir. “Nine times out of ten, we caught the whole gang.”

Van Mechelen rose through the ranks of the BOB until he was head of an entire division. His men loved him; working for him meant plenty of action and also freedom. “There was basically no discipline,” said Guy Verhemeldonck, a former officer who later became the godfather to two of Van Mechelen’s children. (Van Mechelen had two children in the 1980s with his then-partner, and one in the 1990s after marrying another woman.) Sometimes the men had to work long hours, even pull night shifts. Other times they would leave the office in the middle of the day to grab a drink. When they did, Van Mechelen only reminded them to keep their eyes and ears open—after all, criminals hung out in bars, too.

For proof they needed to look no further than the kidnapping of Baron Charles-Victor Bracht, a diplomat, businessman, and multimillionaire. On March 7, 1978, a masked, armed man grabbed Bracht in an Antwerp garage where he’d just parked his Jaguar. The suspect, who called himself “Dexter” when communicating with authorities, asked for more than $2 million in ransom and refused to give proof of life. About a month after the abduction, he called a local newspaper and said that Bracht was dead. One week later, the baron’s body was found in a garbage dump, badly decomposed. Officers aired the perpetrator’s voice to the public, and someone recognized it as belonging to Marcel Van Tongelen, an electrician with a criminal record. But when officers showed up at his parents’ house—Van Tongelen’s registered address—they said they hadn’t seen him in years.

Van Mechelen and his men hit the bars. Armed with a name and a photograph, they went from one establishment to another around Antwerp, looking for anyone who knew the man behind the voice. An officer eventually found a mail carrier who looked at the suspect’s photo and recognized someone he occasionally had a beer with, although he knew him by a different name. The mail carrier pointed officers toward the broad avenue where the man lived. They knocked on the door of every flat until they found the suspect, four months after Bracht’s abduction.

Van Mechelen made liberal use of informants, a practice that was common among Belgian police and largely unregulated at the time. When he caught a criminal, he sometimes offered to help them avoid a harsh sentence if they provided information. “I loved working with Van Mechelen,” a one-time informant told us. “He always offered protection.”

A former member of the judicial police once said that Van Mechelen’s informants “almost seemed like [his] colleagues.” But no one considered it a problem. After all, it was hard to argue with Van Mechelen’s results.

title: The Temperamental Nature of Alligator Gender-Reveal Parties - Nautilus
content:
Human embryos grow at a comfortable temperature just a bit warmer than the mother’s body. Reptile embryos, however, are at the whim of outside temperatures. And, in many cases, the sex of the offspring is known to be decided by incubation temperature.  

In fact, a recent study published in the Journal of Experimental Biology found that the sex of American alligators (Alligator mississippiensis) is set by just a one- or two-degree difference. With environmental temperatures on the upswing, that could make for lopsided alligator populations.

Read more: “Animals Are More Rational Than You Think”

“Whenever a population is out of balance, it can impact population growth,” explained senior study author Benjamin Parrot, an ecologist at the University of Georgia. “If temperatures are biasing sex ratios, that’s a big issue.”

Researchers collected 145 gator eggs from seven wild gator nests at the Tom Yawkey Wildlife Center in North Carolina. Eggs were incubated in the laboratory under five different temperature conditions: 30°C, 31°C, 32°C, 33°C, or 34°C. Several weeks into their incubation—when sex is known to have been established—embryos were removed from eggs to determine sex based on their reproductive structures.

The development of viable embryos didn’t vary between the temperature treatments, but the sex did. The lowest and highest temperatures favored females, while the medium temperatures favored males. At the higher temperatures, just a degree or two could shift the sex. The results also showed that brief spurts of heat expected to damage the embryos—up to 35.6°C—instead boosted their chances of being female.

With wild alligator nest temperatures predicted to rise to as hot as 33.5°C by 2100 across their range, expect some truly gender-bending gator trends in the future.

title: This 150-Million-Year-Old Bird Had a Body Built for the Land - Nautilus
content:
Lots of birds aren’t built for flight: chickens, penguins, emus, etc. This new species of bird (Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis), which lived around 150 million years ago, is another such odd duck (so to speak), though it boasts the added cachet of challenging the conventional understanding of bird evolution.

The traditional view has been that natural selection prioritized characteristics that help birds fly across the millennia. But Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis had a body built more for living on land than in the air. For example, its fossil had sharp teeth, relatively short wings, and a claw on its foot for attacking predators. It’s very much like a small, predatory dinosaur, and experts believe it may not have been able to fly at all.

And yet, it has bird-like features that put it firmly in the Avialae part of the animal kingdom—the evolutionary group where you’ll find modern birds and the extinct relatives closest to them.

“When we examined Yuezhuornis, we were struck by its extraordinary mix of features,” Wang Min, one of the authors of the study on Y. yangyuanensis, explained in a statement. “It possesses bird-like pelvic and hindlimb structures yet retains the specialized predatory foot and teeth of a small meat-eating dinosaur. It shows us that early bird evolution was far more complicated than we previously realized.”

Either the ancestors of this bird could fly, and this species lost the ability, or the entire lineage was never able to take flight in the first place, indicating that flight evolved more than once in early birds.

The incomplete but well-preserved fossil was recovered in southeastern China and is estimated to have come from a bird about the size of a crow—with a mass of around 1.8 pounds. Its anatomy was compared to other dinosaurs and birds of the same time period, as well as modern species, to see where it might fit on the grand evolutionary timeline. All of the evidence points toward a terrestrial lifestyle in the Late Jurassic.

It was around this epoch that flight evolved for the first time, so the dating matters, but experts still aren’t sure how the ability to fly originated. There are theories that it evolved from predators who launched attacks from elevated positions, or from bipeds who started jumping further and further distances while running, or from animals who ran up steep inclines and used early versions of wings to help.

Whatever the reason, given the carnage and chaos that happened on land during the Late Jurassic, it’s no wonder evolution nudged some creatures into the sky.

title: Pinot Noir: Inside the Criminal Gangs Making Fake Wine
author: Peter Rubin
content:
While wine fraud has been around for nearly 150 years, it exploded around the turn of the century, with enterprising counterfeiters drawn by high margins and relatively low risk. Now, though, with the highest-end manufacturers upping their game, would-be forgers are looking at more moderately priced targets; they’ve even come for mass-market brands like Yellow Tail. For 1843, William Ralston uncorks the zero-somm game.

Other popular anti-counterfeiting techniques used by high-end wineries include manufacturing proprietary bottle shapes and micro-printing, where text and patterns are printed at a scale visible only under magnification. (I was shown a bottle of 2009 Le Pin, a fine Bordeaux wine, where the names of the winery owner’s children had been micro-printed repeatedly between two thin red lines on its front label.) Some wineries have adopted advanced security measures, incorporating features like holograms, individualised digital tracking codes and inks that change colour when tilted. Pétrus, a Bordeaux winery which produces only 30,000 bottles a year, uses inks custom-made by the same company that produces the ones used on American dollar bills.

title: Rays of Wonder
author: Brendan Fitzgerald
content:
Hanna Saltzman sets a captivating history of radiology alongside that of her family, generations of medical professionals who championed the benevolent powers of x-rays and radiation and also suffered their damages. Her essay for the new issue of Virginia Quarterly Review wrestles with the impossibility of perfect vision and the inadvertent harms we visit on those who we most want to protect.

Within months of Röntgen’s discovery, the unintended consequences of the X-ray began to emerge. In Tennessee, a boy came to the hospital after an accidental gunshot wound to his head. To test the equipment before trying it on his patient, his physician first conducted a prolonged X-ray of his own head. Three weeks later, the physician lost his hair. That same year, a New York doctor conducting X-ray experiments on himself noticed that his fingernails had stopped growing, his knuckles burned, and even the skin of his hand began to peel away. Blisters bloomed on other people’s bodies—on their hands and arms and chests. Thomas Edison started feeling cramps in his stomach; his vision began to blur. His glassblower, Clarence Dally, tested the quality of the fluoroscope tubes through daily X-rays of his own body. His hair started falling out, and his eyelashes and eyebrows burned away. His hands became red, swollen, and ulcerated. Knobs of deformed tissue bulged from his fingers. A biopsy of Dally’s pinky revealed cancer.

. . .

When Edison saw Dally’s tumors, he swore to never again expose himself or anyone else to radiation. In the year before Dally’s death, as the doomed glassblower lost himself to the disease, the New York World ran a story on the gruesome costs of this celebrated breakthrough. “Don’t talk to me about X-rays,” the prolific inventor told the reporter. “I am afraid of them.”

title: Why Immigration Agents Don’t Quit in Protest
author: Seyward Darby
content:
Before he became an author and professor, Francisco Cantú was a border patrol agent. He’s written extensively about his experience, and here, he tries to understand why more of his one-time colleagues haven’t quit as the second Trump administration has ramped up its draconian immigration enforcement:

Officers are acculturated to see migrants as entirely unlike them, despite the fact that more than half of Border Patrol’s twenty-one thousand agents and nearly a third of ICE’s twenty-two thousand agents are Latinos, many only a generation or two removed from their own family’s migration. They come to think of migrants and asylum seekers as potential gangsters, rapists, or petty criminals, whose asylum claims are almost always suspect, their stories exaggerated to take advantage of the freedoms and generosity of the state.

It’s one thing to theorize about this dehumanization but something else to hear it plainly acknowledged by the people enacting it. One former Latino colleague who still works as an agent told me that, at the height of COVID, “we were deporting everybody, and there was this mother who coughed on me in front of her kids, and I was like, ‘Don’t fucking cough on me!’ ” He shook his head recalling the encounter. “It was like a seesaw battle—I’m yelling, then I’m apologizing, then I’m giving all these people food, then I’m saying, ‘Shut the fuck up.’ ” After a pause, he continued, “You see these people like cattle. So I remember I went home and I cried. You don’t want to treat humans like that.”
